sections.html:
• Common name: Lucky bamboo
  • Scientific name: Dracaena sanderiana
  • Tank size (minimum): any
  • Difficulty: Easy
  • Optimal lighting: Moderate
  • Optimal pH: 6.5 – 8.0
  • Water hardness: Soft to moderately hard water
  • Optimal temperature: 16 – 27 °C
  • Substrate: Any
  • Growth rate: Slow
  • Placement in tank: Midground and background
  • Size: up to 150 cm
  • Fertilizer: Not needed/low
  • CO2: Not needed
  • Propagation: Cuttings

Interesting fact: In some cultures, Lucky bamboo is said to bring love, health, luck, and many other positive things to anyone who owns it. The significance varies according to the number of stalks: two stalks represent love, whereas five stalks represent wealth and longevity.

Lucky bamboo is a species of flowering plant in the family Asparagaceae, native to Central Africa. It is predominantly grown in China and Taiwan and is associated with Feng Shui, an Asian practice which dates back 4000 years. It is common in Central and West Africa and East Asia (India and China), but is now cultivated around the world as a houseplant.

Bamboo is a diverse group of evergreen perennial flowering plants of the family Poaceae, subfamily Bambusoideae. Despite the similarities, Lucky bamboo belongs to a different family from the true bamboo.

Scientific classification: Kingdom: Plantae; Clade: Tracheophyta; Clade: Angiospermae; Order: Asparagales; Family: Asparagaceae; Subfamily: Nolinoideae; Genus: Dracaena; Species: Dracaena sanderiana.

The species was named after the German-English gardener Henry Frederick Conrad Sander.

The plant stays fresh and evergreen if grown in proper conditions: bright illumination, good substrate, soft water and warm temperatures. In its natural habitat, lucky bamboo grows under the canopy of trees, so it can survive well without direct sunlight, like many other indoor plants such as Syngonium.
There is no minimum tank size. Lucky bamboo can be kept in any tank, even nano tanks, as long as it sticks out of the top. Water depth depends on the size of the container.

Lucky bamboo is one of the easiest species to maintain in an aquarium. Place it in moderate, indirect light, as it will burn in direct sunlight.

In a freshwater aquarium, fill the bottom with a small-grained nutrient-rich substrate and put soft pebbles or sand on top as a second layer. Add enough water to completely cover the roots and the lower part of the stalks.

Change the water every week, replacing about 25% with clean fresh water. Use only RO or distilled water. If you still use tap water, dechlorinate it first, otherwise the plant will turn yellow on contact with chlorine.

Since the plant grows slowly, you may only need to prune the stalks a few times a year. Cut just above the nodes with sharp scissors.

Planting

The stalks can be placed as a bundle or spaced apart (about 7 – 10 cm from each other). Placing them apart is better for the root system, and the shape of lucky bamboo offers a beautiful contrast in aquariums.

  • Partial submersion (recommended): the leaves and upper growth are kept out of the water. Choose a healthy, mature specimen of adequate length, bury about 5 cm in the substrate, then fill the aquarium to about 2.5 cm below the lowest leaf set.
  • Full submersion: the entire plant is underwater. It will survive for many months if it gets ample nutrients and CO2.

Full submersion: the plant can survive underwater, but surviving and thriving are not the same. The leaves will discolor and melt, the stalk will start rotting and there will be no growth. It can stay submerged for months but eventually shows signs of deterioration.

Propagation

Lucky bamboo propagates vegetatively. To propagate:

  • Choose a healthy, dark green stalk and cut off the offshoots (at the nodes) precisely to avoid jagged edges.
  • Remove the bottom leaves (the bottom part will sit in water).
  • Place the stalks (partially submerged) in a container of water. The cuttings will form red roots within 30 days, and can then be placed in the substrate.

Alternatively, cut the main stem between the nodes and place the cutting (partially submerged) in a new container of water until it develops roots.

Tip: to protect the cut from pathogens, seal the end of the stalk with candle wax.

Problems

  • Yellow or brown leaf edges: caused by too many nutrients, poor water quality (tap water) or direct sunlight. Avoid over-fertilizing and exposure to direct sunlight and chlorine.
  • Yellow or soft stalks: result of unclean or impure water; the yellow part is almost or already dead. Remove it from the green stalks as soon as possible so the healthy ones are not affected.
  • Fungal diseases: a powdery white coat or small dark spots with red margins on the stem and leaves indicate fungus. According to a study, a bamboo plant became infected with a specific fungus 30-45 days after inoculation, which can grow on stem or foliage. Cut off infected leaves to prevent spread, and separate the healthy part of the stem from the rest.

Sometimes, to save lucky bamboo, you need to cut and re-root it. It will survive.

Temperature: 16 – 27 °C is ideal; in most cases room temperature suits it.

pH: 6.5 – 8.0.

Hardness: although very sturdy, it appreciates soft water and GH between 1 – 5.

Water type: do not use tap water. Lucky bamboo does not like the chemicals in tap water (chlorine, fluoride, etc.). Use only RO or distilled water.

Salinity: according to a study, Dracaena sanderiana can tolerate a low level of salinity, but it is not recommended for brackish setups.

Humidity: it is resilient to humidity fluctuations, but around 50% or higher is recommended. If humidity is very low, mist the leaves every couple of days.

AquaTome's note: RO or distilled water on its own is for lucky bamboo kept by itself. Where fish, shrimp or snails share the water, use dechlorinated tap water, or RO water with minerals added back: animals need minerals that pure water lacks.

Lighting: lucky bamboo does not need much light. It adapts to a wide range of lighting but grows best in low to moderate, indirect light. It can be so tall that it does not fit under the lighting system, in which case it gets only ambient room light.

Substrate: it is very versatile. It roots very strongly and thrives in a nutrient-rich substrate, but almost any substrate can be used. It can also be grown bare-rooted in water or other root-promoting media. If grown hydroponically, it requires a great deal of mineral nutrient solution in the water.

Important tip: lucky bamboo gets nutrition through its roots, so do not use a substrate that prevents this. Sand is in most cases poorly aerated and does not let the plant get nutrients freely; if sand is used, mix it with soil as the bottom substrate.

Recommended soil substrates: ADA Amazonia aqua soil, Carib Sea Eco-Complete, Seachem Fluorite.

CO2: not required if grown emersed (partially submerged). When completely submerged, it needs a high amount of carbon dioxide to survive underwater, so CO2 injection helps.

Fertilizers: being a slow grower, it needs only a few drops of fertilizer every month or two, and possibly none at all, since waste from fish, snails, frogs, shrimp, etc. is used for growth. If you keep shrimp with lucky bamboo, note that a high level of CO2 and copper (most fertilizers contain copper) is extremely dangerous to shrimp.

It is an evergreen, thin, erect shrubby plant. It can reach a maximum height of 150 cm, with leaves up to about 23 cm. The leaves are often twisted and green.

Interesting fact: Dracaena spp. absorb chemicals in the air (such as formaldehyde, trichloroethylene, benzene and CO2) and remove up to 87% of volatile organic compounds every 24 hours.

Difference between Lucky bamboo and true bamboos

  • Appearance: many bamboos have very tall, rigid stems, whereas lucky bamboo has fairly tall, sometimes curvy or flexible stems.
  • Structure: unlike the thick, rough stem of true bamboo, lucky bamboo has a fleshy stem that is not too hard.
  • Growth rate: some true bamboo species can grow as much as 120 cm in 24 hours, while growth in lucky bamboo is very slow.
  • Requirements: true bamboo requires soil, whereas lucky bamboo can thrive in water alone. Many true bamboos also need direct sun each day.

Tankmates

Lucky bamboo can be harmful to pets if ingested, but it does not secrete toxic chemicals into the water. Because of its shape and structure, it is highly unlikely that any fish, snails or shrimp can ingest it, so it can be kept with other animals that cannot tear it up and eat it.

Avoid: most crayfish and freshwater crabs. They will cut, eat and uproot everything in the tank, so unless you let the plant float, it is a no-go.

Quarantine

Commercial bleach is very effective for sterilization in in vitro propagation. Quarantine lucky bamboo before putting it into the aquarium if necessary, because:

  • The plant can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • It could also be treated with pesticides to remove parasites, snails, etc. These chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.

Conclusion

This species gives a unique and premium feel to the aquascape of freshwater tanks, and helps create a forest look which fish and invertebrates will like to navigate.
